one_liner: a marketplace for booking local home-repair pros
one_liner_variants: an app to connect homeowners with people who fix stuff around the house
a two-sided marketplace where homeowners request home repairs (plumbing, electrical, handyman) and independent local pros accept jobs, get paid through the app, and get reviewed
kind of like Thumbtack but just for home repairs in my city
persona: Founder bootstrapping a local home-repair marketplace in one city. Practical, not technical, cares most about trust and safety since strangers come into people's homes. Wants a lean first version but won't compromise on background checks and holding payment until the job is done.
persona_variants: Founder bootstrapping a local home-repair marketplace in one city. Practical, not technical, cares most about trust and safety since strangers come into people's homes. Wants a lean first version but won't compromise on background checks and holding payment until the job is done.
Operations person for the marketplace who is risk-averse, wants everything spelled out precisely, and worries about liability and disputes before anything else.
Fast-moving founder who is impatient, wants to launch in weeks, and is happy to let the tool default anything that doesn't touch money, safety, or trust.
truth: This is a two-sided marketplace connecting homeowners who need home repairs (plumbing, electrical, handyman work) with independent local service providers (mp_supply_type: services) — the platform itself is a single business (tenancy: single_org), not something resold to other companies. Homeowners and providers both create their own accounts (user_accounts: multi_user), with the founder and a couple of support staff having elevated admin powers (roles: owner_staff). Both sides sign themselves up (invite_flow: self_signup) using email and password (identity_provider: email_password). Anyone can browse listed providers and their services without an account, but you must sign up to book or contact someone (external_access: portal; mp_listing_visibility: public_browse, so listings are public content). Homeowners must have an account before they can book (mp_buyer_accounts: account_required); once in, they can create requests, message, and manage their own bookings end to end (client_portal_scope: self_service). Providers don't just sign up and start listing — they apply and the platform reviews and approves them before they can take jobs (mp_seller_onboarding: apply_and_approve), including a background/ID check (mp_identity_verification: sellers_verified) since they are entering people's homes; homeowners themselves just need a working email. Once approved, a provider's listings go live right away, but the platform can flag, hide, or pull them down if there's a problem (mp_listing_approval: live_then_moderated). Buyers mostly find providers by searching near them on a map (mp_discovery: map_location), since this only works when the provider is genuinely close to the job (mp_geography: local_with_distance); everything is confined to one metro area for now (localization: single_locale). Pricing isn't a fixed list — a homeowner describes the job and gets a quote back (mp_pricing_control: quote_per_request), and nothing is confirmed until the provider actually accepts the request within a time limit (mp_transaction_mode: seller_accepts). Money is central: the platform collects the homeowner's payment up front, holds it in escrow, and releases it to the provider only after the job is marked complete (mp_payment_flow: held_then_released), which means payments flow through the app in both directions, in and back out (payments_in_app: payouts_too). The platform makes money by taking a straight percentage commission out of each job (mp_fee_model: commission), and pays providers out automatically as soon as each job is completed rather than in weekly batches (mp_payout_timing: on_completion). If a homeowner and provider disagree — a job wasn't done right, or wasn't done at all — either side can open a dispute and platform staff review it and can issue a full or partial refund (mp_disputes: platform_mediates). Both sides rate each other after the job (mp_reviews: two_way): homeowners want to know a provider is reliable and safe, and providers want to flag difficult customers too. To keep people from taking the relationship off-platform and dodging the commission, in-app messaging only opens up once there's an actual booking between them (mp_messaging: in_app_after_order) — no messaging before that. Cancellations follow a simple rule: homeowners can cancel free within a short window before the job, but a provider who cancels on short notice gets penalized against their standing (mp_cancellation: buyer_window_seller_penalty). Repairs happen in person at the homeowner's address (mp_fulfilment: in_person) — nothing ships and nothing is delivered online. The platform sends the homeowner a receipt and gives each provider a simple earnings statement (mp_seller_tax_docs: platform_receipts) rather than handling full tax-form paperwork for them. Providers get a dashboard showing their upcoming jobs, earnings, payouts, and rating (mp_seller_dashboard: earnings_dashboard). There are no discounts, coupons, or paid placements in this first version (mp_promotions: none), and categories — plumbing, electrical, handyman, and so on — are a fixed list the platform controls rather than something providers can add to (mp_taxonomy_control: platform_fixed). On the more generic side: notifications go out by both email and text (notifications: email_sms) since a job might need same-day scheduling; the app is used mostly from a phone, in a browser rather than an installed app (platform: web_mobile_first); it only needs to work online (offline: online_only); providers and homeowners can attach photos to a job — a photo of the leak, say — but nothing fancier (attachments: basic). The platform launches with a fresh, empty database (data_import: fresh_start) and stays small for a while, a few hundred providers and their jobs (data_scale: small), with a basic CSV export if someone needs their data out (data_export: csv_export) and nothing hard-deleted, just archived (deletion: soft_delete). A simple created/updated-by audit trail is enough (audit_trail: basic), edits happen one at a time so last-write-wins is fine (concurrency: last_write_wins), and data is kept indefinitely (retention: forever) since it's ordinary business data, not health or financial records needing special handling (compliance_sensitivity: ordinary). The founder wants a basic dashboard of totals — jobs done, money moved, active providers (reporting: basic_dashboard) — and lets providers customize their own profile with a photo, bio, and some branding, but nothing deeper like custom fields (customization: branding_templates). The platform connects to a small number of key outside tools — a payments processor and maps/geocoding (integrations: a_few_key) — and sends automatic reminders, e.g. a job is coming up tomorrow, without any other recurring automation (recurring_scheduled: reminders_only). Because listings are public content, the marketplace is also public-facing (public_facing: public_content). Providers need the platform's sign-off before they can take jobs, which is why there's a single-approver step baked into onboarding (approval_workflow: single_approver).

rules: A provider cannot accept jobs until the platform has approved their application
A homeowner's payment is held until the job is marked complete, then released to the provider
In-app messaging between a homeowner and provider only opens once a booking exists between them
A provider who cancels a confirmed job after the cancellation window counts against their standing
A review can only be left by a party with a completed job with the other side
Platform staff can hide or remove a live listing at any time
non_goals: Multi-city or multi-country operation at launch
Discounts, coupons, or paid featured placements
Full tax-form / 1099 filing handling for providers
